name: Home bakery business
blurb: Bake cookies, cakes or bread at home and sell to local customers, within food laws
title: Home Bakery Business: How to Start a Cookie Business Legally
description: How a home bakery or cookie business makes money, the food rules to check where you live, what you need, the risks and how to test demand with a pre-order.
h1: How to start a home bakery business
answer: A home bakery bakes cookies, cakes, bread or treats in your own kitchen and sells them to local customers through pre-orders, markets, social media or local shops. You earn the gap between your price and ingredients, packaging and your time. The catch is that selling food from home is regulated, and the rules differ a lot by country, state and city, so you must check what is allowed before you take your first order.

sections.h: How a home bakery makes money
body: You sell per item, per box or per custom order. Custom cakes and decorated cookies earn more per hour than plain bakes, while bread and simple cookies rely on regular repeat orders.

Ingredients and packaging are the obvious costs; the less obvious ones are your time, delivery, wasted batches, market stall fees and any permit or inspection fees. Many home bakers underprice because they do not count their hours.

ul: A clear answer on the law where you live. In the US, "cottage food" laws vary by state and usually limit home bakers to lower-risk foods that do not need refrigeration; California, for example, requires a county permit and bars dairy and meat products. In the UK, the Food Standards Agency says anyone regularly supplying food must register free with their local authority at least 28 days before trading, and officers may inspect your home kitchen. Other countries have their own registration or licensing rules.
Food hygiene knowledge; some places require a food handler certificate.
Labels with ingredients and allergens where required.
Reliable equipment, storage space and packaging that keeps products fresh.
Liability insurance, and checks on whether your lease, mortgage or home insurer allows a home business.
A way to take orders and payments, such as a simple order form or social media page.

sections.h: Who it suits (and who it doesn't)

head: Suits
Not for
rows: Consistent bakers who can repeat a recipe exactly
People who bake only when inspired
Someone with a local network or social following
Places where home food sales are not permitted
People happy to work evenings and weekends around orders
Anyone unwilling to deal with allergens and hygiene rules

ul: Selling without the right registration or permit can lead to fines or being shut down; check first.
Allergens: a mislabelled allergen can seriously harm a customer, so label and separate carefully.
Underpricing: popular orders can still lose money once your time is counted.
Seasonality: holiday peaks are intense and quieter months follow.
Limits on scale: home kitchens, cottage food caps and your own energy cap output; growth may mean renting a commercial kitchen.

sections.h: How to test it cheaply first

ol: Look up the home food rules for your exact location and confirm what you are allowed to sell.
Bake your best product for friends, colleagues or neighbours and ask for blunt feedback.
Cost one batch fully: ingredients, packaging, energy and your hours.
Take a small pre-order round from people outside your close circle.
Check what local bakeries and other home bakers charge for similar items.
Complete the registration, permit or licence your area requires, and arrange insurance.
Choose a short menu of products you can make consistently.
Design labels with ingredients, allergens and any statements your rules require.
Open pre-orders with fixed pickup or delivery days to avoid waste.
Record costs, hours and orders, and adjust prices after the first few weeks.

faq.q: Do I need a licence to sell baked goods from home?
faq.a: Usually some form of registration, permit or licence is required, but it depends on where you live. In the US, cottage food laws differ by state, and in the UK you register with your local authority. Check your local rules before selling.

faq.q: Can I sell cookies online from home?
faq.a: Sometimes. Some places only allow direct, local sales by home bakers, while others allow shipping within a state or country. Confirm what your rules permit and use packaging that keeps products safe in transit.

faq.q: What sells best for a home bakery?
faq.a: Products that travel and keep well, such as cookies, brownies and some breads, are easier to sell than delicate cream cakes. Custom orders for birthdays and holidays often bring higher prices.
